Mary Henry is enjoying the day by riding around with two friends but everything goes wrong when challenged to a drag race and their car gets forced off of a bridge. The car sinks into the murky depths, and all three women are assumed drowned. Some time later Mary emerges unscathed from the river. She tries to start a new life by becoming a church organist but Mary finds herself haunted by a ghostly figure that instills fear and dread into her. You can find more information regarding this film on its IMDb page. The director Herk Harvey was also a prolific industrial/educational filmmaker for Centron Productions. Another reviewer on Archive.org rightly remarked that the film had a 'purgatorial' feeling. Purgation is without any doubt, to me, the central concern of this film. 
   To understand this, you must first look to the title. 'Carnival of Souls' tells us, very obviously, of a carnival with souls in it that appears in the film. However, there is much greater significance than that. The word 'Carnival' comes from an Italian expression meaning 'removal of meat' (hence the cognate 'carnivore'). Why would a celebration be referred to as the 'removal of meat'? Because when it came about, the world was Catholic; before Lent began, you would want to have a huge gathering where all the meat would be consumed.
   Now you probably see where I'm going. The whole film, as a purgatorial film, is concerned with the removal of the meat--of souls! In other words, the detachment of souls, or rather a very particular soul, from the flesh, from bodily existence. This soul, naturally, is our dear Mary Henry. 
   This principle explains why, as the film carries on, she gradually finds herself detached
more and more from the normal activities of bodily existence, and she likewise finds herself fading out of existence to those who exist in normal, fleshy lives. This is all a gradual removal of the meat, a stripping of Mary Henry for her lent--Purgatory itself, if we accept this symbolism--which is revealed in the horrific climax outside the Carnival.
   Note, further, that she is herself attracted to the carnival. She also has little problem with detaching from reality; she desires it. It is her proper state to be outside the world of the flesh, yet her ignorance leaves her a part of it. Her interactions with the world are unnatural. They consequently feel vile, base, and uncomfortable, even for the viewer. The epitome of the base, vile, and uncomforting in this film is Mr. Linden, whom Ebert called 'a definitive study of a nerd in lust.'
   Nevertheless, Linden cannot be so easily dismissed. He is intricately involved in the Carnival (in the technical sense of the term) for Mary Henry. His attempts to draw Mary further into the life of the flesh must needs be rejected by her; they are repulsive. When she finally does give in slightly, she's even more repulsed, even pushed towards insanity. Linden is representative of the seduction of the flesh and fittingly is a repulsive creature; absolute sleaziness incarnate. His only concern is sexual intercourse with Mary, which he is disturbingly open about.
   All of the characters in the film likewise take a role in the Carnival. They have souls and flesh, but they are all unconsciously involved in the removal of Mary's flesh. I will not take the time to go through each of them; such richness is yours to discover through repeated watchings of this classic.
   I do, however, wish to address Mary Henry herself. It is very telling that her name consists of both a female name and a male name. If you know a bit of Greek, you will know the term 'androgynous' just means 'male female.' Why does it matter? Some people have erroneously tried to cite Mary as a lesbian heroine, which she is not. In her life, she may have been either heterosexual or homosexual, but it does not matter for the film--she's dead! The flesh is no longer of meaning for her. So why call attention to the name? It makes her an Everyman. Both men and women are encompassed within her. Everyone who watches this film is partially seduced into being Mary, partially expected to, and also it is expected that Mary will already be you.
   Thus brings me to the title of this review. This is, at the core, an existential horror. We need no slasher with a mask; existence is the horror. I would be surprised if Harvey had not read a work by Albert Camus or perhaps Jean-Paul Sartre to produce this film. The tensions of existence amongst others for Mary, that is for Everyman, is beautifully displayed in the crisp monochrome. Where the horror is really captured, though, is the gradual fading from existence. Being stripped away in this carnival of souls, having one's substance slowly substracted--that is true terror.
   As I said, this film merits repeated watchings. I say that about most films, it's true, yet I hope my review will have convinced you that I am fully justified in saying it again; nay, fully convinced you to watch it again as soon as you can to learn the depths of the film, and perhaps even of yourself through Mary.

I saw this film as a child on local tv and the dancing spectre sequence in the abandoned amusement park haunted my dreams. Years later, Carnival Of Souls enjoyed a well deserved critical re-appraisal, and was once again made available. Now downlodable it still disturbs. Despite it's low budget and unknown cast, this film sustains an ambience of creeping unease that most FX heavy big budget films can't seem to manage. The keys to this film's power is the minimalist direction of industrial-short film maker Herke Harvey and the extraordinary performance of it's lead actress Candace Hilligoss, whose fearful eyed mounting dread at the increasingly macabre unreality around her propels this film way beyond it's B-movie status. A masterpiece of horror.

"Carnival of Souls" has a good plot and some interesting dialogue, but the film is ruined by incompetence, including a cast that cannot act, and a director that cannot direct. 

It's been claimed that this movie inspired "Night of the Living Dead" and the work of Tim Burton and David Lynch, but I find all of these claims highly unlikely.

I must admit, this movie is brilliant. It starts out pretty slow and gives the immediate impression of a "teen movie", but that picks up after on a couple of minutes. And from there, the ride just goes on.

Candace Hilligoss was perfect for the role of Mary Henry. There is something really disturbing about her looks, beautiful mind you, but with an almost insane impression. As if she "don't belong in the world".. 

Footage, scenery, angles.. so amazing. The scene in the car, with the face in the window was amazing, and the actual carnival is pure art, dance macabre. The movie gives an impression of something intimate, as if we are "along for the ride", not knowing what will happen, or where we will end up. And it is a ride of mild terror, not scary enough to make us worry, but terrible enough to make us tremble in fear.

This is a movie I could watch over and over again. And again.

This film is a masterpiece of film art. Not only is CARNIVAL OF SOULS one of the finest supernatural movies ever made, but it's one of the finest moving image items on the Internet Archive. This hand-made work of genius shows what can be done by a small group of creative people with the imagination to craft something fresh, the dedication to commit to the work, and the persistence to see it through to the end. Kid filmmakers today resort instead to cheap shocks, gore aplenty, toilet humor, nudity, sexual violence, and computer generated special effects and rubber monsters. Sad for them, but with CARNIVAL OF SOULS available here for free, a great gift and a reason to rejoice for us.

I don't believe this film has anything remotely to do with the "night of the living dead" or any other "zombie" movie. Mary Henry is the only person who can see the phantoms, and if anyone is "living-dead" it is her alone.
While Carnival of Souls will never make the mainstream lists of best "horror" movies, I think it is a masterpiece. You have to look at this film in context: it was purportedly made on a shoestring budget and with a small crew. Yet, the photography and music is superb. Note the parallel imagery of the bridge arches and the church arches, for one example and, as another example, the intrusion of the decadent carnival waltz on the spiritual organ piece, juxtaposing the competing dynamics of the new and frightening dimension Mary finds herself thrust into.
This film is notable in its capacity to create an eerie, otherworldy atmosphere with limited resources. It also features some subtle humour, even though I don't think it was meant to be funny overall. The first element of humour is introduced when Mary tries to clear the theme music from her car radio- quite funny.
What is very effective also is the contrast between the rusticity of the setting, in an ordinary town of ordinary people, and the developing strangeness of Mary's personal world.  
The horror itself is developed through the medium of dread; dread that a person can be  caught somewhere between life and death, in a perverse reality where any path our doomed heroine takes leads to a dreadfully undesired outcome - and this is surely the ultimate horror any of us could face.
 No gory or blood-drenched horror film can match the mood of sheer desolation in Carnival of Souls. This is a psychological rather than physical expression of horror, describing the experience of something like purgatory; of a person having her emotional and physical attachment to the world inexorably stripped away. 
Mary is emotionally and spiritually dead and only the memory of shopping can bring her to something like human feeling: a woman's ultimate refuge! Yes, there is sardonic humour in this scenario. Sadly, though, for our Mary, there is no refuge, not even in shopping. 
 Mary Henry is faced with an excrutiating dilemma: go with the (apparently) normal living people, whom she can no longer relate to emotionally or even physically, or go with the dead, whom she is repulsed by. Deciding at last to join the dead is a decision she makes out of a sense of inevitability, having seen her unwanted suitor, Mr Linden, transform into the dead man who had been following her everywhere. Yet this choice is truly horrifying, and, realising that, she attempts to flee the dancing dead - in vain, as it turns out. 
There is the element of dark humour again, in that both a living man and a dead man want the same thing: to dance with her and have sex with her. Mary no longer shares the sexual tensions of the living but is strangely attracted to the derelict carnival site where the dead man hangs out. Note that during the chase scene she laughs at one point, as if some part of her craves such a fate. Macabre but brilliant!
The final dance sequence is the culmination of the plot and, to me, the crowning glory of this film (the car death scene at the end is just a way to complete the circle). When Mary returns to the carnival the final time, she gets a ringside seat at her own damnation: she sees her soul waltzing with the dead man and his cohorts: the "danse macabre", demonstrating that no-one escapes death, no matter how clear and sunny the daylight seems to be.

reviews.reviewbody: This is more of a ghost story than a horror film as such, but this was an original story for the time. Influences on films such as Night of the Living Dead have been mentioned, but elements of "Drag me to Hell" are recognisable here also. Although the characters who encounter Mary in the film all remark on her apparent coldness and she realizes that there is something holding her back from interacting normally with the world, you can´t help a certain emotional involvement with her and her predicament. There is some very effective camera work, particularly of the abandoned amusement park, and the "small town" atmosphere was convincing. (I actually like looking at the cars in these old films). No doubt some director may be thinking about a remake, b ut that would be a shame, because we would no doubt just get a lot of "Wow" special effects in place of good acting. only one grumble, the sound quality was not very good.

So for the idiot who said the influence shows, I should point out there was no mention of this film by anyone connected with film including Romero. Only after this film became a wrongheaded cult film in the mid 1980s did anyone make such claims! Given that the film only receieved limited drive in showings in the midwestern US, it is unlikely Romero or any of the principals had ever heard of it.

If you want to see the films that influenced 'Night', watch 'Invisible Invaders' and 'The Last Man on Earth'.

The claim that this influenced Night is pure fiction! That being said, this film has great atmosphere, and Candace Hilgoss has incredible charisma!
reviews.reviewtitle: This film DID NOT inspire 'Night of the Living Dead'

reviews.reviewbody:
This is a 'must see' for three reasons:
1)This is an eery film that works because of the B&W and also because of the hauntingly creepy organ soundtrack. 
2) This is the only film in which you can see the interior and dashboard of an early 1960's Chevrolet Impala
3) Candace Hilligoss is so beautiful. Those eyes!

Only after a second viewing did this film strike me as odd but in a good way. Movies like this seldom make sense and are somewhat flawed, but nevertheless, this one is truly creepy. The ballromm dancing scene toward the end is quite disturbing, makes no sense whatsoever, has little to do with the plot but adds to the strange feeling this film left with me. Having said that I should point out that most of the scenes are hard to figure out-that being the genius of the movie. A perfect example of that is the organ music in the church-is the music horrific because she is dead? Or because the church or the pastor think she is evil-it could go so many ways-I would never want all movies to be like this but this one shines with it's ability to make you think.

Watched this recently again as I was looking for a public domain movie that would work well for a 3D conversion project that I had planned. The film is still spooky and left this particular viewer feeling unsettled for a few days after the viewing. It still works today and creates a great eerie atmosphere, aided in no small part by gene Moore's excellent organ Music soundtrack and a creepy perfromance by Candace Hilligoss. 
Look out for the upcoming 3D trailer which I will upload in anaglyph format here very soon.

I do not know if Claude Chabrol was aware of this film before directing "Alice ou la derniere fugue" in 1977.
There are obvious differences across both films, but a viewer would realise what I mean by 'revisiting it'...

Herk Harvey made a slew of films for Centron films which did educational shorts. Here, he makes a feature film. There's an edited down version of this which was commercially released which for me is probably as lousy as the pre 1976 version of Touch of Evil. Key scenes of character development and even suspense are trimmed just in those 6 minutes. I suppose getting it under 80 minutes to serve it up with The Devil's Messenger was too damn important.

The soundtrack is excellent too. It's almost all organ music save only for a couple scenes of incidental music. This made the movie feel very claustrophobic and draws you into Mary Henry's plight. 

It's a shame Harvey didn't build off of this picture. I blame the poor handling and distribution for that. He got his acclaim for it late in his life but I think he saw how difficult it was to market movies. You work hard, invest and get no return for your work then back to Centron for films about cleanliness so that you can afford to eat. Shame..

reviews.reviewtitle: Genuinely frightening and clearly influenced Romero
reviews.reviewbody:
This film scared the life out of me when I saw it on TV in the 70’s, where it often played on various UHF channels (I saw it on Chicago’s channel 32). The sheer unworldly power of Mary’s journey, her isolation from the living, her helplessness- it’s unlike anything else I’ve seen. There is some wooden acting from minor characters - although the landlady, the rapey neighbour and the doctor are all pretty great and as others have said here, Hilligoss is top notch - but for the most part everyone is moving in the same direction, towards Mary’s genuinely horrific end. 

Romero has clearly stated that it was an influence on him, as have Lynch and James Wan. Anyone who claims to know better is just armchair commenting (an odd argument to make, in my opinion), based on their own weird biases. The film played mostly in drive-ins but was well seen across the Midwest and went on to be a staple of late night and Saturday afternoon horror movie rosters.

Mary Henry ends up the sole survivor of a fatal car accident through mysterious circumstances. Trying to put the incident behind her, she moves to Utah and takes a job as a church organist. But her fresh start is interrupted by visions of a fiendish man. As the visions begin to occur more frequently, Mary finds herself drawn to the deserted carnival on the outskirts of town. The strangely alluring carnival may hold the secret to her tragic past.
